extracted.intended_audience: owners/operators of electric generating units (EGUs), power plant designers and operators, state/tribal regulators, environmental compliance professionals, industry stakeholders and commenters
extracted.subtask_description: Federal New Source Performance Standards (NSPS) guidance and final rule rationale for stationary combustion turbines (base load, intermediate, and low load), including the EPA's determination of the Best System of Emission Reduction (BSER), numerical emission limits, compliance metrics, and considerations used to set and adjust standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-component BSER for base load combustion turbines (Phase 1 and Phase 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For base load combustion turbines the EPA is finalizing a two-phase BSER: Phase 1 = highly efficient generation combined with best operating and maintenance practices; Phase 2 (beginning in 2035) = continued use of highly efficient generation and best O&M practices coupled with 90 percent capture CCS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phase 1 implements numeric standards representative of best-performing EGUs in each subcategory. Phase 2 reduces the emissions rate by 89 percent to reflect a CCS system capturing 90% of emitting CO2 when the turbine is operating. EPA rationale and timelines are explained in the preamble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-component BSER for low and intermediate load turbines
rubrics_metrics.description: For intermediate load turbines the BSER is the most efficient available simple cycle technology in combination with best operating and maintenance practices; for low load turbines the BSER is the use of lower-emitting fuels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These single-component BSER determinations support the specific numeric standards finalized for intermediate and low load subcategories and are applicable from May 23, 2023 for low/intermediate load turbines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase-1 numeric standard — large base load combustion turbines
rubrics_metrics.description: Final phase-1 standard of performance of 800 lb CO2/MWh-gross for large base load combustion turbines (those with a base load heat input rating greater than 2,000 MMBtu/h).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standard is based on demonstrated performance of existing high-efficiency combined cycle EGUs, normalization for design/configuration differences, and estimation at lower capacity factors to provide an achievable nationwide never-to-exceed standard with an acceptable compliance margin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase-1 numeric standard — small base load combustion turbines
rubrics_metrics.description: Final phase-1 standard of performance of 900 lb CO2/MWh-gross for small base load combustion turbines (those with a base load rating of 250 MMBtu/h).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA considered best-performing small units (e.g., Holland Energy Park) and accounted for potential efficiency improvements and normalization (cooling, configuration) to conclude a 900 lb CO2/MWh-gross standard is achievable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase-1 numeric standard — base load turbines sized between 250 and 2,000 MMBtu/h
rubrics_metrics.description: For base load combustion turbines with base load ratings between 250 MMBtu/h and 2,000 MMBtu/h the emissions standard is between 900 and 770 lb CO2/MWh-gross based on the base load rating of the EGU.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA proposed a sliding/scale approach across the size range; the preamble explains how size-based scaling was derived from fleet data and normalized performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase-1 numeric standard — intermediate load turbines
rubrics_metrics.description: Finalized standard of performance of 1,170 lb CO2/MWh-gross for intermediate load (variable/peaking) simple cycle combustion turbines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA evaluated performance data for simple cycle EGUs installed since 2015, accounted for design choices (aeroderivative vs frame, water injection vs dry low NOx), and selected 1,170 lb CO2/MWh-gross as achievable across manufacturers and designs without requiring the most efficient variants exclusively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase-1 numeric standard — low load turbines (fuel-based)
rubrics_metrics.description: For new and reconstructed low load combustion turbines the BSER (use of lower-emitting fuels) supports a standard ranging from 120 lb CO2/MMBtu to 160 lb CO2/MMBtu depending on the fuel burned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA proposed these fuel-based standards to apply at all times; the preamble discusses applicability by fuel type and compliance calculation units (lb CO2 per MMBtu).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance calculation: 12-operating-month rolling average
rubrics_metrics.description: Compliance with the standards of performance is to be determined on a 12-operating-month rolling average basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA calculates the 12-month CO2 emission rate by dividing the sum of CO2 emissions by the sum of gross electrical energy output over the same 12-operating-month period. EPA favored long-term averages because NSPS is a never-to-exceed standard and long-term data account for degradation and variable operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of long-term (maximum 12-month) data to identify achievable emissions rates
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA used the lowest maximum 12-operating-month emissions rate for each unit (from 2015–2023 CEMS data) to identify long-term lb CO2/MWh-gross emission rates demonstrated by the existing fleet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long-term averages account for degradation and variable operating conditions; EPA concluded long-term demonstrated rates are more appropriate than short-term peaks or single-year values for setting a never-to-exceed standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjustment for fuel other than natural gas (fuel-relative scaling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Owners/operators burning fuels other than natural gas may elect to use the ratio of the heat input-based emissions rate of the specific fuel(s) burned to the heat input-based emissions rate of natural gas to determine a source-specific standard of performance for the operating period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA provided an example: the NSPS emissions rate for a large base load combustion turbine burning 100% distillate oil for the 12-operating-month period would be 1,070 lb CO2/MWh-gross. Phase-2 CCS standards are similarly adjusted based on uncontrolled emission rates relative to natural gas (example: 100% distillate oil = 120 lb CO2/MWh-gross).

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalization for design/configuration and cooling technology
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA normalized reported emissions to account for probable differences in future new-unit designs: increased reported emissions by 1.0% for combined cycle EGUs using dry cooling (versus cooling towers) and increased by 1.4% for single-shaft (1-on-1) configurations relative to 2-1/3-1 multi-shaft configurations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These normalization factors adjust demonstrated emission rates to be more representative of a nationwide standard that must accommodate various design choices (cooling, shafting) and to avoid disadvantaging units likely to be built in space-constrained or water-limited regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting for operating load and capacity factor effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Emission rates vary with operating load: combined cycle CO2 emissions are lowest at roughly 80–90% load and increase at lower loads; EPA modeled impacts of duty cycle and estimated achievable emissions at lower capacity factors (e.g., 40% 12-operating-month capacity factor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA binned hourly data by load and season to isolate impacts; because low-load hours have less influence on the 12-month average (emissions summed over total output), EPA estimated emissions at lower capacity factors using trends to ensure standards are achievable for EGUs that operate at lower duty cycles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative-unit selection and rejection of outliers for national standard-setting
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA did not base the nationwide standard on atypical individual units (e.g., Okeechobee Clean Energy Center) that are not representative nationally due to configuration (multi-shaft), cooling (recirculating cooling), unusually high duty cycles, or other factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA explained reasons for excluding or not using certain low-emission outliers: differences in shaft configuration, cooling technology, operation primarily at high duty cycles, and possible lack of accounting for long-term degradation. Standards are based on representative fleet performance, not exceptional outliers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of normalization and capacity-factor extrapolation to set standards achievable at lower duty cycles
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA used trends of increasing emission rates at lower 12-operating-month capacity factors to estimate emissions at a 40% 12-operating-month capacity factor for best performing units so the standard is achievable even where more low-load operation might occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA plotted 12-month emissions versus 12-month heat-input-based capacity factor and extrapolated to lower capacity factors rather than simply excluding low-load hours from the calculation, because low-load hours have limited impact on the 12-month average but can still affect compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of commenters' concerns about ambient conditions, starts/stops, and operational variability
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters argued that site conditions (climate, elevation), cooling choices (dry cooling), start/stop cycles, backup fuel use, degradation, and automatic generation control can affect achievable emissions and recommended more flexible standards or higher emission limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA responded by analyzing seasonal and load effects (finding minimal seasonal temperature impact on combined cycle emission rates) and by using long-term averages and normalization to account for these operational variabilities; EPA rejected approaches that would unduly weaken the standard while concluding the finalized standards are achievable with proper maintenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase-2 CCS percent capture selection and commenters' solicitation
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA determined that 90% CCS has been demonstrated and is appropriate for base load combustion turbines, and used an 89% reduction to set CCS-based phase-2 standards (reflecting 90% capture operational whenever the turbine operates); EPA solicited comment on a reduction range of 75–90%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA considered availability/reliability, startup characteristics of CCS vs turbine, and practical capture operation. The preamble discusses cost, capture performance, and policy considerations supporting 90% capture as the Phase-2 BSER component.

rubrics_metrics.name: IRC section 45Q tax credit eligibility as a consideration for CCS feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility for the IRC section 45Q tax credit for existing EGUs requires design capture rates equivalent to 75% of a baseline emission rate by mass; sources with partial capture rates below that would not be eligible and lower capture rates receive smaller tax-credit returns tied to the amount sequestered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA used the tax credit eligibility and its impact on project economics to support selecting 90% capture (partial capture would sequester less CO2 and likely be more costly per ton sequestered and might foreclose tax credit eligibility for some projects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconstruction and retrofit technologies as compliance pathways
rubrics_metrics.description: Reconstructed stationary combustion turbines can use manufacturer upgrade packages (e.g., GE Advanced Gas Path, Siemens Hot Start on the Fly, Solar Turbines compressor restaging) and retrofit options (steam injection, HRSG additions) to increase output and efficiency and comply with intermediate or base load standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA provided examples and cost/size guidance (e.g., steam injection equipment estimated at $250/kW and up to 60% smaller than a similar HRSG), and cited examples of simple-cycle to combined-cycle conversions (e.g., Riverton Unit 12, Energy Center Dover) to show practicable retrofit paths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of hybrid power plants and solar augmentation as not part of BSER
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA is not including hybrid power plants (integration of solar thermal/CSP with fossil-fired EGUs) as part of the BSER because of gaps in knowledge about costs, concerns about cost-effectiveness, limited geographic suitability (DNI constraints), and small expected CO2 reductions relative to costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA summarized NREL and other analyses (e.g., integrated CSP LCOE reductions, small percent generation contribution, land and DNI constraints) and commenters' failure to provide new cost information supporting cost-effectiveness; EPA therefore excluded hybrids from BSER.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of combined heat and power (CHP) as not part of BSER
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA did not propose CHP as the BSER because CHP requires that a facility primarily generates thermal output and have a proximate, consistently operating thermal host with sufficiently large thermal demand—constraints that limit applicability, size, geographic availability, financing, and long-term reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA explained CHP applicability is typically to smaller EGUs (several hundred MW max), requires reliance on the thermal host for the life of the EGU (risk if host shuts down), and can create funding difficulties and pricing pressures; these practical limitations led EPA to reject CHP as BSER.
